prompt: You typed your password into a page you now suspect was fake. What is the first thing to do?
options: Change the password on the real site from a trusted device, then report it
Wait to see whether anything happens
Clear your browser history
Restart your computer and carry on
explanation: Speed matters. Changing the password takes the stolen one out of play, and reporting lets others be protected.

prompt: The password you typed is also used for your email and your shopping accounts. What do you do?
options: Change it on every account that uses it, starting with email
Change it on one account only
Add a digit to the end of it everywhere
Nothing, because they will never try the others
explanation: Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites. Email comes first because it can reset almost every other account.

prompt: Why is a unique password for each account recommended?
options: One stolen password cannot unlock your other accounts
It makes signing in faster
Browsers require it
It stops all phishing
explanation: Unique passwords limit the damage of any single theft. A password manager makes them easy to live with.

prompt: Your phone keeps showing sign-in approval prompts that you did not start. What should you do?
options: Deny them all, change your password and report it
Approve one so the prompts stop
Ignore them
Turn off your phone and do nothing else
explanation: Someone has your password and is hoping you will approve out of annoyance. Deny every prompt and secure the account.

prompt: A website offers to turn on two-step verification. What is the best response?
options: Turn it on, preferably with an authenticator app or security key
Leave it off because it takes longer
Turn it on and email the codes to IT
Only turn it on when travelling
explanation: A second step blocks most account takeovers. Codes are personal and must never be shared with anyone.

prompt: You clicked a link in a suspicious email at work, but nothing seemed to happen. What now?
options: Report it to your IT or security team right away
Say nothing, because nothing happened
Wait until Monday
Delete the email and forget it
explanation: Harm is often invisible at first. A quick report lets the security team check your device and warn colleagues.

prompt: Why is reporting a phishing email useful even if you did not click?
options: It lets the security team protect colleagues who received the same message
It gets the sender fined
It speeds up your computer
It is only needed if money was lost
explanation: Attackers send the same message to many people. One report can stop the others from being caught.

prompt: You paid an invoice to bank details from a fake email and realised the next day. Who do you contact first?
options: Your bank, immediately, to try to stop or recall the payment, then your security team
The sender of the email
A friend
Nobody, because it is too late
explanation: Banks can sometimes stop or recall a payment, but only if they hear quickly. Contacting the sender only warns the fraudster.
